data.title: Qoidalar — all the course rules in one checklist
data.subtitle: All the rules of weeks 5–7 in one place, grouped under four themes

narr: Welcome to this comprehensive guide covering the essential rules for Weeks 5 through 7 of your Introduction to Engineering course. We'll organize all these principles into four key themes to help you master the problem-solving process.
Let's begin with the first theme: problem framing.

data.heading: 6.1 Rules of problem framing
bullets: Sort what you hear: fact, inference, speculation, opinion — only facts and good inferences can anchor the statement.
A problem statement names the need, not the solution: no device, no app, no vehicle (the solution-free test).
Variables are measurable quantities with units: performance (what we judge), design (the levers), context (the limits).
Works well is defined by the stakeholders — write the performance down in numbers.
The statement template: [Stakeholder] needs [outcome] in [system], judged by [measure], within [constraints].
The working definition of performance: the performance of [the system] is judged by [variables with units and targets], through the eyes of [the stakeholders].

narr: When framing problems, first sort what you hear into facts, inferences, speculations, and opinions. Only facts and good inferences can anchor your statement.
Remember that a problem statement should name the need, not the solution. Avoid mentioning specific devices, apps, or vehicles - this is what we call the solution-free test.
Variables must be measurable quantities with units. We categorize them into performance (what we judge), design (the levers we can adjust), and context (the limits we must work within).
The definition of works well comes from stakeholders. You must translate this into numerical performance metrics.
Use this statement template: [Stakeholder] needs [outcome] in [system], judged by [measure], within [constraints].
Here's our working definition of performance: the performance of [the system] is judged by [variables with units and targets], through the eyes of [the stakeholders].

data.heading: 6.1 Rules of problem framing (continued)
bullets: Goals: must-have = demand, nice-to-have = wish; do not turn a wish into a requirement.
A model is built for one clear question: first the question, then the model.
Every model keeps what matters, discards what does not, and serves the purpose-question; no map is the network.
All models are wrong, but some are useful (George Box): usefulness is decided by the question, not by completeness.

narr: Distinguish between must-haves and nice-to-haves. Must-haves are demands, while nice-to-haves are wishes. Never turn a wish into a requirement.
Models should be built to answer one clear question. Start with the question, then build the model.
Every effective model keeps what matters, discards what doesn't, and serves its purpose-question. Remember, no map is the network itself.
As George Box famously said, all models are wrong, but some are useful. The usefulness of a model is determined by how well it answers your question, not by its completeness.

data.heading: 6.2 Rules of modelling
bullets: Four types of models — physical, graphical, mathematical, computational; real projects mix several types.
The anatomy of a model: inputs (we choose), parameters (we fix), relationships (the rules), outputs (we predict) — each with units.
A model is a machine: numbers go in, a rule is applied, numbers come out; every number needs its units.
The week 4 variables become roles: performance →output, design →input, context →parameter.
Need–Know–How–Solve: How includes the assumptions you make in order to solve the problem; Solve — compute, check the units, interpret.

narr: There are four types of models: physical, graphical, mathematical, and computational. In real projects, you'll often mix several types.
Think of a model's anatomy with four components: inputs (what we choose), parameters (what we fix), relationships (the rules), and outputs (what we predict). Each must have units.
A model works like a machine: numbers go in, a rule is applied, and numbers come out. Every number needs its units to be meaningful.
The variables from week 4 take on new roles: performance becomes output, design becomes input, and context becomes parameter.
Follow the Need–Know–How–Solve framework. The How section includes your assumptions, and Solve involves computation, unit checking, and interpretation.

data.heading: 6.2 Rules of modelling (continued)
bullets: A unit check after Kosky: units cancel like fractions — (u×C) [kWh] ÷ e [kWh/km] = [km].
Three kinds of assumptions: simplifying (we ignore), data (we fix), boundary (we leave outside).
Write every assumption with the template: We assume ... because ... . If it is wrong, ... .
An assumption that is written down can be checked; a hidden one cannot.
Classify the assumptions: Safe — holds under normal conditions; Risky — may fail and change the answer; Need Data — cannot be said yet.

narr: Always perform unit checks after Kosky's method: units cancel like fractions. For example, (u×C) [kWh] divided by e [kWh/km] equals [km].
There are three kinds of assumptions: simplifying (what we ignore), data (what we fix), and boundary (what we leave outside the model).
Write every assumption using this template: We assume ... because ... . If it is wrong, ... . This makes your assumptions explicit and testable.
Remember: an assumption that is written down can be checked, while a hidden one cannot. Transparency is key.
Classify your assumptions as Safe (holds under normal conditions), Risky (may fail and change the answer), or Need Data (cannot be determined yet).

data.heading: 6.2 Rules of modelling (continued)
bullets: Stress-test the model: change one assumption and explain the effect on the output.
Three checks: units, order of magnitude, a known value; ask Is this a reasonable answer? every time.
The cycle: Frame →Build →Check →Revise — repeat until it is good enough for the decision.
The model's verdict: Too Simple / Fit for Purpose / Too Detailed; the goal is fit for purpose: the simplest model that answers the question well enough to decide.
Finish with one revision and one additional need for data.
Every model has a range in which its assumptions are valid: know it and state it.

narr: Stress-test your models by changing one assumption at a time and explaining how it affects the output.
Perform three checks on every result: units, order of magnitude, and comparison with a known value. Always ask, Is this a reasonable answer?
Follow the modeling cycle: Frame →Build →Check →Revise, and repeat until your model is good enough for decision-making.
Evaluate your model as Too Simple, Fit for Purpose, or Too Detailed. The goal is Fit for Purpose - the simplest model that answers the question well enough.
When finishing, include one revision and identify one additional need for data.
Every model has a range of validity where its assumptions hold true. Know this range and state it clearly.

data.heading: 6.3 Rules of quantitative reasoning
bullets: Demand is what the system must deliver; capacity is the maximum it can deliver; both need units and a time basis.
A number without a time basis is as incomplete as a number without units.
Compare like with like: one unit and one time basis on both sides before dividing.
Utilisation = demand ÷ capacity: below ~0.8 — comfortable; around 1 — tight; above 1 — demand is turned away or a queue grows.
Size for the peak, not for the average: the average hides the peak (a 94 kW average against a 180 kW peak at 13:00).

narr: In quantitative reasoning, distinguish between demand (what the system must deliver) and capacity (the maximum it can deliver). Both need units and a time basis.
Remember: a number without a time basis is just as incomplete as a number without units. Always include both.
When comparing values, ensure you're comparing like with like. Use the same unit and time basis on both sides before dividing.
Calculate utilization as demand divided by capacity. Below 0.8 is comfortable, around 1 is tight, and above 1 means demand is turned away or queues grow.
Always size systems for peak demand, not average demand. The average can hide significant peaks, like a 94 kW average compared to a 180 kW peak at 13:00.

data.heading: 6.3 Rules of quantitative reasoning (continued)
bullets: kW is an intensity, kWh is an amount; power × time = energy.
Carry the units in square brackets: 60 [kW] × 2 [h] = 120 [kWh]; the units check both the method and the answer.
Change in stock = inflow − outflow; when positive, something is accumulating (a queue, a buffer, a battery).
The flow rules (flow = speed × density; number inside = arrivals × time) hold only under steady-state conditions.
The bottleneck is the stage with the smallest capacity; it sets the system's maximum practical throughput.

narr: Remember that kW is a measure of intensity (power), while kWh is a measure of amount (energy). The relationship is power multiplied by time equals energy.
Always carry units in square brackets throughout calculations. For example, 60 [kW] multiplied by 2 [h] equals 120 [kWh]. The units verify both your method and your answer.
The change in stock equals inflow minus outflow. When this value is positive, something is accumulating - whether it's a queue, a buffer, or a battery.
Flow rules like flow equals speed multiplied by density, or number inside equals arrivals multiplied by time, only apply under steady-state conditions.
Identify the bottleneck as the stage with the smallest capacity. This bottleneck determines the system's maximum practical throughput.

data.heading: 6.3 Rules of quantitative reasoning (continued)
bullets: Estimate before calculating: identify the quantity and its units → break into factors → round each factor to one digit and multiply → check the units and compare with a known value.
An order-of-magnitude estimate is correct to within a factor of ~10 and often better: 21 barbershops against 23 in the directory.
Bound the estimate: low / typical / high; if the decision does not change across the range — stop refining (23–38kW → still a rooftop installation).
Precise is not the same as correct: one–two significant figures; about 30 kW, not 29,17 kW.
Most estimation errors are errors of units or of counting: confusing kW and kWh, the forgotten peak, double counting, false precision.

narr: Before calculating, always estimate: identify the quantity and its units, break it into factors, round each factor to one digit, multiply, then check units against a known value.
An order-of-magnitude estimate is typically correct within a factor of about 10, and often better. For example, estimating 21 barbershops when the directory shows 23.
When estimating, provide bounds: low, typical, and high values. If your decision doesn't change across this range, stop refining. For example, 23-38kW still suggests a rooftop installation.
Precision is not the same as correctness. Use one to two significant figures. Say about 30 kW, not 29.17 kW.
Most estimation errors come from unit mistakes or counting errors: confusing kW and kWh, forgetting peaks, double counting, or presenting false precision.

data.heading: 6.3 Rules of quantitative reasoning (continued)
bullets: When an answer looks strange, check the units and the time basis first (0,2MW = 200 kW; 36 min = 0,6h).

narr: When an answer seems strange or unexpected, first check your units and time basis. For example, remember that 0.2 MW equals 200 kW, and 36 minutes equals 0.6 hours.

data.heading: 6.4 Rules for working with incomplete data and making decisions
bullets: Name the data problem first: too little, missing, noisy, out of date / unrepresentative, wrong definition / unit — the fix depends on the type.
Five sources of numbers: measure, look up, ask, estimate, analogy — with different levels of trust; write the source and the confidence next to every number.

narr: When dealing with incomplete data, first identify the specific problem: is it too little data, missing data, noisy data, out-of-date or unrepresentative data, or wrong definition/unit? The solution depends on the type of problem.

Numbers come from five sources: measurement, looking up values, asking experts, estimation, and analogy. Each has different levels of trust. Always write the source and your confidence level next to every number.
